title: Origins: The Portuguese and the Sugar Model
bullets: Portuguese caravels probing south past Cape Bojador in the 1430s opened the African coast to Europe; in 1444 an expedition brought enslaved Africans back to Lisbon, the conventional start of the maritime slave trade.

The Portuguese did not conquer West Africa — the kingdoms were too strong, the diseases too lethal — so they built fortified posts like Elmina (1482) and dealt with African rulers as trading partners for gold, ivory, and people.

On the equatorial island of São Tomé around 1500, the Portuguese first welded plantation sugar to enslaved African labor at scale, inventing the murderously profitable template that Brazil, the Caribbean, and the American South would all copy.

After Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas split the non-European world between Spain and Portugal, setting the legal scaffolding for an Atlantic system of African supply and American demand.

As Indigenous labor collapsed under the encomienda and European epidemics — over ninety percent dead on some islands — the Spanish turned to Africa; the first enslaved Africans reached Hispaniola by about 1502, the true start of the transatlantic trade.
The asiento, first issued in 1518, made the delivery of human beings a coveted, taxed, regulated government monopoly — the trade was a licensed branch of state commerce from very early on.

King Afonso I of Kongo, a Catholic convert who embraced Portugal as an ally, protested in the 1520s that traders were seizing free subjects and depopulating his kingdom; his pleas to control the trade were ignored, the demand too strong.

Bartolomé de las Casas, denouncing the abuse of Indigenous people, early on suggested importing enslaved Africans instead — a recommendation he bitterly repudiated; the European debate asked not whether slavery was wrong but which people could justly be enslaved.

By 1550 every piece was in place: a proven sugar model, surging American demand, organized African supply, and an emerging ideology placing Africans at the bottom of a hierarchy of who counted as fully human.

title: The System Scales: Brazil and the Caribbean
bullets: From around 1550 Brazil planted sugar along its northeastern coast in engenhos worked, after Indigenous labor collapsed, by enslaved Africans; Brazil would import close to five million people, more than ten times the number ever brought to what became the United States.

The Dutch West India Company (1621) broke the Iberian monopoly, seizing Elmina and holding sugar-growing northeastern Brazil for a quarter-century, then carried the complete technical know-how of plantation sugar to the Caribbean.

Tiny Barbados, switching to sugar and enslaved labor around the 1640s, became within one generation the richest English colony in the world — the first and purest case of the 'sugar revolution' the whole Caribbean would copy.

On the sugar islands enslaved people died faster than they were born, the population shrinking unless constantly topped up off the ships — a cold calculation that it was cheaper to work people to death and buy replacements.

England's Royal African Company, chartered in 1672 under the king's brother the Duke of York, branded captives with the letters 'DY' — a measure of how the trade was woven into the very top of the English state.
France's 1685 Code Noir defined enslaved people as movable property in sixty calm administrative articles — proof that Atlantic slavery was not lawless but increasingly, exhaustively legal.

The trade's profits flowed back to European ports — Liverpool, Bristol, Nantes — comfortable towns far from the violence whose prosperity rested on it, spread across a whole society of investors, insurers, and sugar-buyers.

Through slave codes written from the 1660s onward, the colonies invented racial slavery: bondage made lifelong, hereditary through the mother, and tied specifically to African descent — something genuinely new in the history of slavery, and the foundation of modern racial categories.

title: The African Coast and the Kingdoms
bullets: The overwhelming majority of the roughly 12.5 million captives were obtained not by European raids inland but captured, bought, and delivered to the coast by other Africans — a documented fact that the honest account neither erases nor weaponizes.

A chain of forts strung along the shore — Cape Coast Castle, Saint-Louis, the notorious island of Gorée — hinged on the barracoon, the fortified barracks where captives were chained for weeks or months while traders waited to fill a ship.

Luanda, in Portuguese Angola, grew into the single largest embarkation point of the entire Atlantic trade, most of its captives bound for Brazil; in Angola the Portuguese pushed inland and waged war to capture people directly.

Queen Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba fought the Portuguese for nearly four decades, allying and warring by turns and sheltering people fleeing their territory; she dealt in captives like every power around her yet became a lasting symbol of African resistance.

Dahomey, conquering its way to the coast under Agaja in 1727 and institutionalizing the trade under Tegbesu, ran slaving as a royal monopoly through the port of Ouidah — a genuine slaving state, yet arguably as much captured by the trade's gun-for-captive logic as enriched by it.
The Asante Empire and the Oyo Empire, two great West African powers, took captives in wars of expansion and channeled them to the busy ports of the Bight of Benin in exchange for firearms and goods.

A free person became a captive in many violent ways — war above all, plus kidnapping (as the child Equiano was snatched from his Igbo village), debt, crime, and oracle — then was sold and resold hundreds of miles to the coast.

The older trans-Saharan trade ran alongside the Atlantic one for centuries but moved people more slowly, took more women and children, and never reached the Atlantic system's industrial concentration of mostly young men funneled into export crops.

Atlantic Creoles — multilingual people of mixed African and European descent who brokered the trade — show the coast was never a simple wall, and foreshadow the hybrid creole cultures that would flower in the Americas.

title: The Middle Passage as a World of Its Own
bullets: The Middle Passage was the human leg of the triangular trade — Africa to the Americas — endured by the roughly 12.5 million captives, of whom an estimated 1.8 million died in the crossing.

The slave ship was purpose-built as a prison: low platforms doubled the human cargo into two layers with under three feet of headroom, captives chained in pairs, netting rigged over the deck to stop those who tried to throw themselves into the sea.

The six-to-ten-week voyage held captives below in lightless, reeking heat where dysentery, smallpox, and fever killed; the death rate averaged roughly one in seven but swung from a handful to nearly everyone aboard.

Captives resisted constantly — refusing food until crews forced their jaws with a speculum oris, leaping overboard in the belief death would return their spirits to Africa, and mutinying so often that insurers charged extra and ships carried added crew.
The crews suffered too: slaving sailors died at rates rivaling the captives', a fact Thomas Clarkson later used to demolish the claim that the trade was a 'nursery for seamen.'

The holds carried mostly young men but also many women, who faced routine sexual violence, and significant numbers of children; strangers thrown together became 'shipmates,' a bond treated as kinship and the first family many had in the Americas.

In 1781 the crew of the Zong threw more than 130 living chained captives into the sea and filed an insurance claim, exposing in an English court that the trade treated murder as a question of who owed whom money.

Arrival brought sale by formal auction or by the 'scramble' — buyers rushing a pen to grab people — followed by 'seasoning,' the brutal first one-to-three years in which roughly a quarter to a third of new arrivals died, which is precisely why the system had to keep importing more.

title: The Plantation Complex and the Economics
bullets: The Atlantic slave trade was a moral horror and, inseparably, among the most profitable ordinary business of its age — woven into banks, insurance, shipyards, and European breakfast tables — which is why it lasted four centuries.

Sugar was the master crop, but tobacco in the Chesapeake, coffee in the highlands, and rice in the Carolina swamps each extended the system; rice planters specifically prized West African captives for the agricultural knowledge stolen along with them.

The triangular trade bound three continents — goods to Africa, captives across the Middle Passage, plantation produce back to Europe — and the firearms sold on the coast fed a self-reinforcing cycle of guns buying captives and captives buying guns.

Slave-trade wealth was enormous and widely distributed across European society, giving a vast number of respectable, powerful people a direct stake in keeping the trade alive — which is why abolition meant fighting a whole economy, not a few villains.

Law and hierarchy supplied the order: slave codes fused race to lifelong hereditary bondage, while Spanish America's baroque casta system ranked everyone by their precise proportion of European, African, and Indigenous descent.

Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) made short-staple cotton hugely profitable across the American South, exploding the demand for enslaved labor at the very moment the moral campaign was winning and the import trade was closing.

Slave-grown cotton became 'King Cotton,' the United States' leading export and the raw material for the most modern industry of the age, binding the South to the global economy and ensuring slavery would end only in the bloodiest war in the nation's history.

After the 1808 import ban, the domestic slave trade forcibly moved roughly a million people from the Upper South to the cotton frontier in chained coffles — the 'Second Middle Passage' — tearing Black families apart on a colossal scale. The trade no longer needed the ocean; it had come home.

title: Resistance, Revolt, and Marronage
bullets: From the moment the chains went on, enslaved people resisted by every means available — the false image of passive victims is refuted on nearly every page of the record.

Everyday resistance was constant: broken tools, slowed work, feigned illness, sabotage, flight, and the quiet preservation of language, religion, music, and family against a system designed to erase them all.

The grandest resistance was marronage — escape into permanent free communities; in Brazil, Palmares grew into a confederation of quilombos numbering perhaps tens of thousands and defied Portuguese and Dutch power for most of a century.

Palmares' last leader Zumbi, born free there, was betrayed and killed in 1695; the Portuguese displayed his head to prove him mortal, but he became one of the most powerful symbols of Black resistance in Brazil.

Jamaica's maroons, many of Akan origin and led by figures like Queen Nanny, fought the British to a standstill and won formal treaties in 1739–40 — though at the dark price of returning future runaways — making Nanny today a National Hero of Jamaica.
Where escape was impossible, revolt followed: the Stono Rebellion (1739) marched toward Spanish Florida, and Tacky's Revolt (1760) shook Jamaica's planters before both were crushed.

In the United States the conspiracies and risings are remembered by their leaders — Gabriel near Richmond around 1800, Charles Deslondes on the German Coast in 1811, Denmark Vesey in Charleston in 1822, and Nat Turner in Virginia in 1831, whose revolt haunted the South more than any other.

At Christmas 1831 the Baptist preacher Samuel Sharpe led Jamaica's largest revolt, the Baptist War; its scale and the savagery of its suppression landed in Britain as the abolition debate climaxed, helping push emancipation over the line within two years.

Most revolts failed in the narrow sense, but they were not futile: they proved the enslaved would never consent, forced concessions, exposed the system to a watching world, and fed directly into the movement that would end the trade.

title: The Abolition Movement
bullets: For more than two centuries the slave trade was normal — legal, respectable, immensely profitable; in a single generation a determined minority turned it into a moral abomination and built the first modern political campaign to attack it.

The Quakers turned decisively against the trade, disowning members who trafficked in people by 1758, and Quaker schoolteacher Anthony Benezet armed a generation of abolitionists with pamphlets showing Africans as peaceful people unjustly torn from their homeland.

The 1772 Somerset v Stewart ruling, won by activist Granville Sharp, was narrow in law but widely understood to mean an enslaved person who set foot in England became free, electrifying the cause on both sides of the Atlantic.

The 1787 Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade deliberately targeted the trade first and invented modern activism — mass petitions, a consumer boycott of slave-grown sugar joined by hundreds of thousands of households, and propaganda at scale.

Two icons made the horror impossible to look away from: the Brooks diagram, showing human beings packed into a real ship's hold to scale, and Thomas Clarkson's collected shackles, branding irons, and thumbscrews laid before audiences.

Abolition was not a gift handed down by white men: the formerly enslaved Sons of Africa campaigned in their own voices, and Olaudah Equiano's best-selling 1789 narrative told the trade from the inside and made the enslaved a person with a name and a case to make.

In Parliament William Wilberforce introduced bill after bill against the ferocious West India Interest, losing through the 1790s as war with revolutionary France made Parliament fear anything that smelled of dangerous liberty.

After twenty years of grinding failure, the 1807 Slave Trade Act made it illegal for British ships to carry enslaved Africans — abolishing the trade, not slavery — a genuine watershed won by a movement led in part by the very people the trade had tried to reduce to property.

title: Haiti: The Revolution That Couldn't Happen
bullets: Saint-Domingue, the French western third of Hispaniola, was in the 1780s the single richest colony on earth, its sugar and coffee wrung from roughly half a million enslaved people under conditions so lethal the population had to be constantly replenished from Africa.

Because the colony worked people to death so fast, much of its enslaved population was African-born, recently free, and in many cases militarily experienced — the most explosive concentration of enslaved humanity in the Atlantic world.

In August 1791 a gathering at Bois Caïman, remembered as a Vodou ceremony led by the priest and coachman Dutty Boukman, lit a coordinated uprising; the enslaved burned the rich northern plain, and the revolt organized into a sustained revolution rather than subsiding.

Toussaint Louverture, born enslaved and freed before the rising, revealed himself a military and political genius, forging the rebel bands into a real army and maneuvering through a chaos of shifting alliances among planters, free people of color, France, Spain, and Britain.

When revolutionary France abolished slavery in all its colonies in 1794, Toussaint threw his army behind it, driving out the Spanish and British; by the late 1790s a formerly enslaved man governed the richest colony in the Americas.

Napoleon sent his brother-in-law Leclerc with tens of thousands of troops in 1802 to restore slavery; the French lured Toussaint to a parley, seized him, and shipped him to a French mountain prison where he died in 1803 — which enraged the revolution rather than breaking it.
Yellow fever, to which the French had almost no resistance, scythed through Leclerc's army; disease and ferocious resistance together destroyed the largest expedition Napoleon ever sent overseas.

Jean-Jacques Dessalines crushed the remaining French at Vertières in November 1803 and on January 1, 1804 proclaimed independence under the Taíno name Haiti — the only nation on earth ever born of a victorious slave revolt, its founding act the permanent abolition of slavery.

The slaveholding powers punished Haiti for the achievement — refusing recognition for decades and forcing a crushing indemnity to compensate the defeated slaveholders — but nothing could undo the proof, written in fire, that the enslaved could free themselves.

title: The Slow Legal End
bullets: Outside Haiti, slavery ended slowly, unevenly, and by law — country by country over most of a century — when moral campaigners, the enslaved's own refusal, shifting economics, and great-power interest all pushed in the same direction at once.

The first dominoes were trade bans: Britain in 1807 and the United States in 1808, which cut off the ocean supply but did not end slavery — in America the ban arrived just as cotton exploded the demand for labor, turning the trade inward.

The British Royal Navy patrolled the West African coast for decades intercepting ships, while smugglers ran captives to Cuba and Brazil; in 1839 Africans aboard the Amistad rose under Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué) and won, in 1841, a Supreme Court ruling that they were free.

Britain's 1833 Slavery Abolition Act freed roughly 800,000 people, but paid twenty million pounds in compensation to the slaveholders — nothing to the freed — and bound most to years of unpaid 'apprenticeship,' revealing whose interests the law protected.

In the United States the cause was carried by Black abolitionists above all: Frederick Douglass, who escaped Maryland in 1838 and became abolition's most commanding voice, and Harriet Tubman, who returned again and again as the most famous conductor of the Underground Railroad.

It took a war: the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) turned the Civil War into a struggle over slavery and opened the army to nearly 200,000 Black men, and the Thirteenth Amendment (1865) finally wrote slavery out of the Constitution.
Brazil, the largest slave society of all, ended slowly — an 1850 law closing the Atlantic import under Royal Navy pressure, the 1871 Law of the Free Womb, and partial measures freeing the elderly.

As enslaved people deserted the plantations faster than the legislature could act, Princess Isabel signed the 1888 Lei Áurea, or Golden Law, abolishing Brazilian slavery outright with no compensation and no apprenticeship — freeing the last legally enslaved people in the Western Hemisphere.

title: The Surviving Cultures
bullets: The Atlantic system was designed to erase the people it enslaved — their names, languages, families, and gods — and it failed, because the captives carried their cultures in the one place the traffickers could not search: inside themselves.

Faced with masters who demanded they become Catholic, enslaved Africans matched their own deities to Catholic saints — a process called syncretism — so they could go on worshipping the old powers in plain sight, behind a mask the master could not see.

That concealment produced a family of living Afro-Atlantic religions: Vodou in Haiti, woven into the revolution itself; Candomblé in Brazil, built around the Yoruba orixás; and Santería in Cuba — faiths with millions of adherents today, not curiosities on life support.

Thrown together speaking many unintelligible languages, the enslaved forged wholly new creole languages combining European vocabulary with African-influenced structure, like Haitian Creole and the Gullah tongue of the South Carolina and Georgia Sea Islands.

The relatively isolated Gullah retained more of their African inheritance than almost any other U.S. community — a distinct creole language, rice-centered foodways, sweetgrass baskets woven the West African way, folktales, and naming practices.

African drumming, call-and-response, polyrhythm, and improvisation crossed in the bodies of the enslaved and became the foundation of the blues, gospel, jazz, and samba — a lineage running directly from the holds of the ships to the world's popular music.

Foodways and craft crossed as durably as faith and music: okra, black-eyed peas, and yams reshaped the cooking of two continents, and ironworking, woodcarving, pottery, and textile traditions carried African knowledge into the Americas.

These cultures survived through immense loss — specific languages, lineages, and names severed forever — which is what makes them remarkable: the enslaved did not merely preserve old cultures but created new ones from broken pieces, a victory the traffickers could never undo.

title: The Afterlife and the Reckoning
bullets: A law can end a practice in a moment but cannot undo four centuries of consequences; when Brazil signed the Golden Law in 1888 the trade was legally over everywhere, but the world it had made did not dissolve.

The ledger, reconstructed voyage by voyage from some 36,000 records, counts roughly 12.5 million Africans embarked and 10.7 million surviving to land — a floor, not a ceiling, that does not even count those killed in the wars, raids, and marches before the ships.

The trade redistributed those millions in a pattern most people guess wrong: close to five million to Brazil and only a small fraction to what became the United States, whose large enslaved population grew by births while the sugar zones shrank and had to be replenished.

The modern African diaspora is the trade's demographic shadow, still visible on the population maps of two continents — why Brazil has the largest population of African descent outside Africa and the Caribbean is overwhelmingly African-descended.

Atlantic slavery's most insidious legacy was the idea of race itself — a fixed, ranked biological hierarchy that science has thoroughly rejected, built to make the system feel natural and outliving emancipation by generations in segregation and inequality.

Out of the scattering grew Pan-Africanism, which sought to reunite a dispersed people in spirit and purpose, and Négritude, the 1930s literary movement that took an identity the trade had tried to degrade and reclaimed it with pride.

The reckoning remains unfinished: advocates of reparations point to the asymmetry that when slavery ended it was the enslavers who were paid — Britain's slaveholders, the slaveholders Haiti was forced to indemnify — while the stolen were freed into poverty.

The book closes holding two truths at once: the scale of a deliberate, legally organized atrocity, and the truth that the people inside it were never only its victims — they resisted, freed themselves in Haiti, led abolition in their own voices, and built living cultures that flourish to this day.
